name: International Orange (Engineering)
lede: International Orange (Engineering) is the deepest, reddest of three colors called international orange, the one that belongs to engineering specifications rather than to the Golden Gate Bridge or to aerospace.

sections.title: One name, three oranges
sections.body:
The phrase "international orange" traces to the Golden Gate Bridge [1]. Its consulting architect, Irving Morrow, noticed the reddish-orange primer already on some of the steel, and pushed to keep it as the finish color over the Navy's preference for black-and-yellow stripes, when the bridge opened in 1937 [1]. That bridge's own paint is a custom mix, lighter than this one [1]. A second shade, International Orange (Aerospace), is lighter and more orange still, used on aircraft and spacecraft for visibility [1].

This variant, International Orange (Engineering), is deeper and redder than both, defined under Federal Standard 595, the United States government's 1956 paint-color specification for military and engineering contractors, as color FS 12197 [1]. The three share a name and a family resemblance but are not interchangeable paints [1].

Its nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[venetian-red]], almost the same shade; [[carnelian]] sits close by, duller [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for this red-orange in 114 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.48 percent, more common than 64 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 18 of 945 paintings from that century, 2.9 times the rate its share of the archive would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 95 percent of its appearances, which fits a color built for visibility rather than for covering a surface [3].

It is most over-represented in paintings from Italy, at 2.1 times the expected rate [3]. The earliest archive match is dated 1365, in a work by Luca di Tommè; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first, and no fifteenth-century painter was using a paint standardized in 1956 [1][3]. It shares canvases more than chance with the colors we call Dark Chocolate Brown and Rich Black (FOGRA39) [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications [3].

origin.named_after: the "international orange" family of high-visibility colors, first associated with the Golden Gate Bridge (1937); this variant fixed by Federal Standard 595 (1956) as FS 12197

disambiguation.gloss: a different standard orange-red, not this engineering specification

notes.cite: ColorHub archive (23,781 paintings), computed match, as photographed

questions.q: Which structure is most associated with the name "international orange," even though it uses a different custom shade?
True or false: International Orange (Engineering), International Orange (Aerospace) and the Golden Gate Bridge's paint are all the exact same shade.
Why does this color turn up mostly as a small accent in our painting archive, rather than covering large areas?
choices: It is a high-visibility safety color, used in small amounts on purpose
It fades fastest of all reds
It only exists on metal, never on canvas
questions.answer: It is a high-visibility safety color, used in small amounts on purpose

openers: "International orange" is really three different paints wearing one name.
